Brayden looked at the article again. The website mentioned none of that. It called the retraction a "suppression," and the comments below it were vitriolic in a way that made him close the tab of his attention, half a screen at a time. "So it's fake."

"No," Anastasia said, and Peyton winced, because Anastasia had a habit of correcting people in the direction they didn't want. "It's real that it was published. It's real that those authors said what they said. That's the problem. It isn't fake, it's just one paper, and one paper never gets to be the answer. You'd need other people doing the same study and not finding it. Lots of them. Other people checking the work before it prints, and after."

"Peer review," Peyton said.

"Which doesn't catch everything, apparently," Anastasia said, tapping the article, "because this one got through. So then what catches it is everyone else."

Mr. Gill, who had been arranging beakers at the front with the patience of a man waiting out a rainstorm, said nothing, which Brayden understood later was deliberate. Instead Mr. Gill handed him the laptop cart key and said, "If you're going to argue with your mother, you should do it with the good databases." So Brayden spent the last twenty minutes of the period not doing the friction lab, and Peyton sat beside him, and Anastasia hovered, and they found the original paper, which listed its twelve cases in a table so small it fit on a single page, and then they found the retraction notice from 2010, terse and official, and then they found other studies, dozens of them, whole shelves of them, other researchers who had gone looking for the same link in far more children and come back with nothing.

"So when the doctor says it's safe," Brayden said slowly, "he's not saying one guy checked. He's saying everybody checked, and the one guy who said otherwise got his paper taken back."

"That's the whole thing," Peyton said. "That's how it works."

Friday morning his mother drove him to the clinic with the article on the passenger seat, already creased into a defensive posture. In the waiting room she read it a third time, and Brayden said, "Mom, did you know it was twelve kids?" and told her about the retraction, about replication, about the room full of other studies, and he watched her hold on to the paper the way people hold on to a railing. She did not become an apologist for the article, but she did not put it down either. She said she would think about it, which was more than she had said about anything since his father left, and less than he wanted.

The twist came when the nurse called his name and his mother stood, folded the article, and handed it not to the trash can but to Brayden, saying, "Keep it. You're the one going to college. You should know what people are afraid of." He took it. In the exam room, while Dr. Okafor washed her hands, Brayden slid the paper into the side pocket of his backpack, next to the chemistry notes, where it would ride home with him, still folded, still printed, twelve children long.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky's 1988 book Manufacturing Consent argued that news is shaped by five 'filters', the first of which is the ownership of media by large corporations.
story:
The crepuscular light had settled into the corners of the living room by the time Olivia spread the two newspapers across the carpet. One was the Herald, the daily her family had taken since before she could read. The other was the Ledger, a weekly from the next county. Both had covered the school board's vote on the new stadium contract, and the two accounts did not match. The Herald piece ran nine paragraphs and quoted only the board president. The Ledger ran thirty and listed the bids the district had rejected, including one that was four hundred thousand dollars lower.

Agathe came through the doorway with her shoes still on and dropped onto the couch. "You're doing the editorial?"

"Lochlan wants it by Friday," Olivia said. "But I can't figure out why the Herald didn't mention the other bids." She slid the Ledger across the floor. Agathe read it with her chin on her knees.

Lochlan arrived twenty minutes late, holding a paperback with a cracked spine. He had read it for Mr. Vargas's media seminar, the one class where the teacher mostly assigned books and said almost nothing. He sat on the arm of the chair and turned the book so Olivia could see the cover. "Herman and Chomsky, 1988," he said. "Manufacturing Consent. Five filters, and the first one is ownership." He tapped the page he'd folded. "News outlets are owned by companies or people, and that shapes what gets covered."

Olivia looked at him, then at the Herald's masthead, where in small type it named its parent corporation. She had never once read that line. The same corporation, according to the Ledger's archive, owned the construction firm that had won the stadium bid. She wrote the parent company's name on a napkin and underlined it twice.

That evening, Agathe watched Olivia from the kitchen doorway while pretending to refill her water. Olivia had gone quiet somewhere around seven, and Agathe knew what that quiet meant, because she had seen it before the debate final last spring, when Olivia had argued a position she didn't hold and won anyway. Now Olivia was reading the Herald's stadium story a third time, then reading her own draft, then crossing out an entire paragraph with a single line.

"You're not going to say what you think," Agathe said. "You're going to say what's safe."

"I'm going to say what I can prove," Olivia said, and Agathe heard the other sentence underneath it, the one about the paper's adviser, about how the student paper printed what the principal signed off on, about who decided what counted as provable. Agathe didn't push. She sat down and started reading the Ledger's list of rejected bids aloud, slowly, as if for a transcription, and Olivia began to type.

The next afternoon Olivia found Mr. Vargas carrying groceries up his front steps, the same steps he had climbed for thirty years while teaching chemistry, then history, then economics, a polymath who retired into a garden that failed every summer. She asked whether the filters meant nothing in the news could be trusted.

"That's not what the book says," he said. "It says there's a structure. What you do with a structure is your business." He lifted the last bag. "Come by when the editorial runs."

She spent that night deciding, and by morning she had stopped deciding and started cutting. She kept the provable parts: the ownership, the bids, the masthead's fine print. She cut the sentence that called it a scandal, because she could not prove intent, and she was honest with herself that intent was exactly the thing she could not see from inside her living room. Maybe the Herald's reporter was lazy. Maybe the editor was careful. Maybe the structure produced the result without anyone choosing it, and that possibility was the one that kept her sitting on the carpet past midnight, unable to suture the two newspapers into one true account.

Lochlan read the final draft on Friday and frowned at the last line. "It doesn't land anywhere."

"It lands where it lands," Olivia said.

He read it again. "You want me to print that?"

She took the pages back, folded them once, and handed them across the newsroom desk, keeping her hand on them a second longer than she needed to.

"Print it," she said.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Frozen food can be thawed safely in the refrigerator, in cold water or in the microwave, but not by leaving it out on the counter.
story:
Victor's mother left on a Sunday, for ten days of training in another city, and the fridge behind her held a lemon, a jar of mustard, and something in foil that neither of them had been willing to investigate. Before her taxi came she stood at the counter with a pen and said he could order food like a raccoon for ten days, or he could learn to feed himself like a person, and she let him choose, which was her way of not letting him choose. He chose like a person. He wrote "PLAN" at the top of a page and then, after a long moment, "WEEK."

By Tuesday he had a system, or the outline of one. He had read enough to know that cooking in batches was the point: make four portions on Sunday, eat two during the week, freeze the rest for the days after, and never stand in front of the stove on a Wednesday wondering what was for dinner. He made a list, grouped it by aisle so he would not walk the whole store twice, and checked the prices of chicken thighs at three shops online before admitting that this was a form of procrastination. Then he walked to the shop with the list folded in his pocket like a ballot, and in the aisle he found Amina from his chemistry class holding two brands of rice and looking at them as if one of them had lied to her.

"You meal plan now?" she said, when she saw the list.

"I batch cook now," Victor said. "There's a difference. A plebiscite happened. I voted for the version of me with containers."

She put both rices in her basket, defeated, and walked with him while he chose onions, rejecting one that felt soft in his hand with a confidence he did not fully own. He told her the plan: Sunday cooking, portions into the freezer, one moved down to the fridge every night so the next day's meal would be ready to reheat. She said it sounded like something a retired man would do, and then asked him to text her a photo of whatever he actually cooked, as evidence.

Sunday came and Victor cooked. He browned the chicken badly, then better. He made enough rice to feed a small delegation and portioned everything into containers he had found at the back of a cupboard, still dusty from the previous era of the household. The apartment smelled like a place where someone lived. He labeled the containers with a marker, dates and contents, feeling faintly ridiculous and privately proud, and stacked four of them in the freezer, flat, the way a website had suggested, so they would freeze evenly. He moved one container to the fridge for Monday. Monday's dinner was a small, greasy triumph, eaten standing up, and he texted Amina the photo. She replied with a single thumbs up, which he chose to interpret as awe.

The problem arrived on Thursday. He had come home late after Ilan had kept him at the pitch arguing about whether a throw-in counted as a real possession, and he had gone straight to bed without opening the freezer, which meant Friday's container was still in there, a solid brick of stew, and dinner was supposed to happen in an hour. He stood in front of the open freezer, holding the container, and did what he called introspecting, though it mostly looked like standing still. The obvious move was to leave it on the counter and go have a shower. The counter was right there. He set it down. Then he picked it up again.

He texted Ilan, who was no help, and then Amina, who answered while he was still staring at the container. "Don't leave it out," she wrote. "My mum works with food safety. Frozen stuff thaws safe in the fridge, in cold water, or in the microwave. On the counter is the one way that's not safe." He read it twice. The fridge was too slow, he decided, since the brick would still be a brick at dinner. Cold water he could do, submerging the sealed container in the sink and changing the water, but the microwave was faster and he was hungry now, so he put the container in and pressed the defrost button and listened to it hum while he introspected no further.

The thawed stew reheated with a skin on it that he chose to think of as character. He was eating it when a knock came at the door, and it was Mr. Bekele from two floors down, holding a plate of something wrapped in foil, because the whole building, it turned out, had been informed of Victor's situation by his mother before she left. Mr. Bekele had brought food every few days, and Victor had never known what to say, since the man's own cooking smelled better than anything Victor had managed.

"You're eating," Mr. Bekele observed, with what might have been approval or pity.

"I cooked it," Victor said. "Batch cooking. There's a system."

Mr. Bekele looked at the container in Victor's hands, then at the foil plate in his own, and appeared to conduct a brief internal election about what to do with it. He handed it over. "For the freezer, then," he said. "You have a system."

Victor took the plate, and after the door closed he stood in the kitchen holding it, thinking about the small cabinet-level decision ahead of him: whether the gift went into the rotation with the labeled containers, or sat in the fridge on its own, unnumbered, a foreign ministry in his planned state. He wrote on a piece of tape, in careful letters, "Bekele, no date," and pressed it onto the lid.

Then he opened the freezer, slid the plate in flat between two bricks of stew, and moved Saturday's container down to the fridge before he could forget again.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Nitrogen and oxygen make up about 99 percent of dry air but are not greenhouse gases, because molecules made of two identical atoms do not absorb infrared radiation.
story:
The printout kept trying to blow away, so Sara weighted its corners with shells, four of them, dull gray ones she'd chosen because Ayva was saving the spiral shells for her collection. The graph underneath showed a single climbing line, carbon dioxide measured decade by decade, and Sara had until Monday to explain it, along with everything behind it, or take the zero that would sink her grade in Ms. Hoang's class.

"You're staring at it like it insulted you," Ayva said, digging her toes into the wet sand at the edge of the tide. She had wanted to swim since they arrived, and the light was already going long and gold across the water, and her wetsuit was half on, sleeves dangling.

"I am being insulted, sort of." Sara flattened a corner the wind had lifted. "Ms. Hoang said I could explain it to her after school Monday. Out loud, the whole thing. If I can do it, she'll wipe the failed quiz. If I can't, it stands." She'd argued her case for twenty minutes, pointing out that she'd been sick the week of the unit, and Ms. Hoang had listened with that patient stillness of hers before saying, "Make it make sense to someone who's never heard it. That's the test." Then she'd said, "Try the beach, if it helps. Some people think better with their feet in the sand."

Vince was sprawled on a towel with the textbook open on his chest, sunglasses pushed up into his hair. He was the only one of them who'd actually read the chapter, and he wore this fact the way other people wore new shoes. "Want to run through it?" he asked. "You start, I'll tell you where you break."

Sara started with the air itself, because that seemed like the beginning. "So the atmosphere is mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Almost all of it, like ninety-nine percent of the dry air." She paused, gathering the logic. "And those are the gases trapping the heat. That's why the whole thing warms up. There's so much of them."

Vince sat up slowly. He found the page with his thumb before he said anything, which was annoying, the way he always located the evidence first. "That's backwards," he said. "Nitrogen and oxygen make up about ninety-nine percent of dry air, but they're not greenhouse gases. The book's exact about it. Molecules made of two identical atoms don't absorb infrared radiation." He turned the book toward her, one finger under the sentence, and Sara read it twice, the second time slowly, while a wave came in and slid cold around her ankles.

"But that's," she said, and stopped. The counterintuitive part of it sat there refusing to move. The most abundant gases, the ones the air was almost entirely made of, did nothing of the sort. The trapping came from the trace things, the ones too small to see on any pie chart of the sky. She looked back at the climbing line on the graph, the decades of measurements, and for the first time the graph seemed less like an accusation and more like an answer to a question she hadn't known how to ask. Small amounts could matter enormously; the composition and the quantity were different questions entirely.

Ayva had come to stand over the printout, arms crossed against the cooling air, still in her half-wetsuit. She had her own problem, which was that she was testing for junior lifeguard certification on Saturday, and the swimming test would be in cold surf like this, and she'd been told her physiology course notes would help her understand cold-water shock but she'd left them home. "Explain it to me, then," she said. "If I have to stand here not swimming, you have to make it worth it. Explain it like I'm the lifeguard who doesn't care about chemistry."

Sara took a breath and tried. She kept her feet planted where the tide could reach them, because moving somehow made it harder. She talked about the sun's light coming through, and the earth sending heat back up as infrared, and how the air being mostly nitrogen and oxygen didn't matter to that at all, because those molecules were each made of two identical atoms and didn't absorb the infrared. It was the other gases, the sparse ones, that caught it, held it, sent it back down. Then she touched the graph, the whole climbing arc of it. "So this line," she said, "this is the stuff that does the trapping, accumulating. The trace part. Not the big part." She heard how strange the sentence sounded and said it anyway, because it was true, and because Ayva was watching her like the explanation was holding her hostage.

"The water's getting darker," Ayva said finally. "That was almost good. You lost me at the part where you said the trace part, then found me again at the line." She pulled her sleeves up. "One more time and then I'm swimming whether you're done or not."

Sara looked at the graph, at the wind worrying its loose corner, at the impermeable gray sky over the horizon where the light was gathering itself to leave. She thought about what Ms. Hoang had said, that she couldn't promise the retake would change anything on the transcript, that a school couldn't indemnify a student against her own missed week, only offer the second chance itself. Maybe that was the honest position: she could explain the mechanics now, and read the line, and still not be certain she'd hold it all together under Ms. Hoang's quiet listening on Monday. She could be sure of the fact and unsure of herself, both at once, and that was allowed.

She began again, softer, at the beginning, with what the air was almost entirely made of and why that wasn't the point at all, and behind her she heard Ayva counting down from ten, and at three, a wave collapsed loud and white against the sand.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A population pyramid conventionally shows males on the left and females on the right, with age groups stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top.
story:
The room Ms. Harper used for geography had a wall of windows that faced the bus loop, and on Friday afternoons the buses arrived in long yellow lines while the last class of the day was still working. Noah liked that. It gave him something to watch when the worksheet stopped making sense, which it had, twenty minutes ago.

"Question four," Trystan said, sliding the packet across the table. "Kenya. Does the country need more schools or more nursing homes, and how can you tell from the pyramid."

Edmond had already written half an answer, his pen moving in the confident way it did when he wasn't sure of anything. Noah pulled the printed chart toward himself and looked at it properly for the first time. Two columns of horizontal bars, stacked like a staircase, with numbers running up the side. He followed the shape downward with his finger and frowned.

"So the young people are at the top," he said. "That's why it's wide up there."

Edmond kept writing. Trystan looked up.

"No," Trystan said. "Youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top. My cousin told me when she did this course. The bars climb with age, like the stack gets older as it rises."

Noah turned the chart ninety degrees, then back, trying to make the shape flip. The bottom bands were fat and the top ones thin, so the population was young, so schools, so the whole argument Edmond was building on old people at the top was standing on air. Then a second problem surfaced, quieter than the first. The two columns were labeled, one on each side, and Noah had been reading the left column as one thing and the right as another without ever checking which was which.

"Which side is which?" he asked. "Left and right?"

Edmond turned the packet around as if the answer would be different from his side of the table. Trystan leaned over the chart, squinting at the small print.

"Males on the left, females on the right," Trystan read. "It says it right there."

"It does not say that clearly," Edmond said.

"It says it in tiny letters under the axis, which is basically designed to be missed." Trystan tapped the page. "So you were reading the women's bars as the men's."

Noah thought about the bus loop, how you could stand at the far end and the buses looked like one vehicle, and only by walking the line did the gaps appear. He had been looking at the pyramid from the wrong end, and it hadn't felt wrong. That was the part that bothered him. A wrong reading of a chart doesn't announce itself. It just sits there looking like a chart.

"Start over," Noah said, and took out his phone, which Ms. Harper allowed for research as long as it stayed flat on the table where she could see it. He opened his messages. His older sister had emailed him that morning about the fall she'd been on, from a job the library had put her on furlough from, and her note was still at the top of the screen. He read it again before he could stop himself. The furlough might end in October, she'd written, or it might not, and the landlord had already agreed to wait. He closed it gently, the way you close a door on someone sleeping, and typed a search instead.

The results confirmed Trystan without ceremony. Same fact, three sources, stated the same flat way each time. Noah set the phone down and pulled the chart back.

"Okay," he said. "Males left, females right, youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top. That's the whole grammar of it. Once you know that, the shape means something."

Edmond had stopped writing. He was looking at his own half page of neat script, and Noah could see him doing the arithmetic of how much he'd have to cross out. Their friend from chemistry had done the same thing last month with a whole lab report built on a mislabeled axis, and had simply abrogated the results section rather than admit the foundation was wrong. Edmond was not that kind of person, usually. But it was Friday, and the buses were loading, and starting over is a specific kind of tired.

"Everything I wrote is backwards," Edmond said.

"Most of it," Noah said. "The part about the top bands being narrow is still true. You just called them the young ones."

Ms. Harper came down the row, coffee cup in hand, and paused at their table without picking anything up. She looked at the crossed-out paragraph, the turned chart, the three phones lying flat and honest.

"You found the axes," she said.

"He found the axes," Trystan said, pointing at Noah.

"Then write me what you'd build," she said. "Schools or nursing homes, and show me where on the shape you're pointing when you say it."

She moved on. The buses were pulling out, one after another, empty. Noah took a clean sheet and drew the outline of the pyramid freehand, quick and a little crooked, the bottom wide, the top narrow. He marked the bottom with a small S for schools, and beside it wrote that the shape was young, and that the read depended entirely on knowing which end was which. Under that he added one more line, that he trusted the chart itself but not yet his own eye, and that he'd want a second source before he'd argue it out loud.

Edmond copied the fact across the top of his page in careful capitals, so he couldn't lose it again.

"Males on the left," he muttered, underlining. "Females on the right. Who decided that?"

"Somebody in a tiny font," Trystan said, and Noah laughed, and drew the next pyramid before he could forget which way was up.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: ATP synthase works like a tiny rotary motor: protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP.
story:
Brandon had failed the first test so completely that his mother had signed him up for summer tutoring before asking him anything about it, and now Mr. Anderson was coming to the backyard with a shoebox.

"Sit," Mr. Anderson said, pointing at the picnic table, and Brandon sat, because the alternative was arguing, and arguing in June had a way of costing him August. Sloan was already there, sprawled on the bench with the textbook open to a page she had clearly not read, since she was reading it upside down. Mr. Anderson set the shoebox down and took out a hand-cranked flashlight, a length of garden hose, and a plastic pinwheel from a dollar store three towns over.

"Before Tuesday," he said, "you two will be able to trace glucose to ATP without notes. Not because I tell you. Because you build it." He was the chemistry teacher who had retired the year Brandon started high school, and he tutored out of what appeared to be genuine stubbornness rather than money, since he charged ten dollars a session and refused to take it twice when Sloan's mother had tried.

He handed Sloan the hose and told her to lay it in a spiral on the table. "That's your mitochondrion," he said, and then held up the pinwheel. "This is one enzyme inside it. Blow on it." She blew, and it spun, its cheap plastic catching the light. Brandon watched it and felt the familiar humiliation rise, the same feeling he'd had in April when he'd written "ATP comes from food" on the test and Mr. Anderson's replacement had read it aloud as an example of what not to write. He still hadn't decided whether to tell anyone it was his answer.

"Protons," Mr. Anderson said, pointing at the pinwheel. He made Sloan crouch and blow through the hose so the air came out at the blades at an angle, and the pinwheel turned faster. "Inside you, right now, ATP synthase works like a tiny rotary motor. Protons flowing through it make part of the enzyme spin, and that motion builds ATP." He said it once, then made Sloan repeat it, then Brandon, then Sloan again, while she blew and the wheel spun and the water in Brandon's glass trembled slightly in the table's rhythm.

That was the whole demonstration, apparently, because Mr. Anderson then took out index cards and made them map the rest from the book: glucose broken in the cytoplasm, the small molecules ferried into the spiral of hose, the slow accounting of what was gained at each stage. It was, Brandon noticed, a way of thinking he hadn't tried before. He had dichotomized the subject into things to memorize and things to give up on, and the pinwheel refused both categories. It was a machine. It had a mechanism he could watch. When Sloan spun it with her finger and said, "So the ATP is basically being assembled by something turning," Mr. Anderson only shrugged, which Brandon was beginning to understand was how he said yes.

Sloan left at five to work a shift at the pool, and Brandon stayed because his mother had paid for the hour and forty minutes remained. He turned the pinwheel with his finger and thought about whether wanting to understand something was different from wanting the grade. He suspected the second was extrinsic, something bolted on, and the first was not, but he couldn't be sure he'd have cared at all if a test hadn't shamed him first. The shame had come first. That was the part he couldn't rearrange.

Mr. Anderson was packing the box when he said, without looking up, "The kid who wrote 'ATP comes from food.' That was you, wasn't it."

"Yeah," Brandon said, and waited to be told something about perseverance or effort, some verdict. Instead Mr. Anderson handed him the pinwheel. "Take it. Tape it above your desk." He closed the box, and his expression gave away nothing, which meant Brandon would have to decide for himself, over the summer and after, whether what he'd learned in the backyard was knowledge or just a plastic wheel he could make spin.

He carried it home in his back pocket, and when his mother asked from the kitchen how the tutoring had gone, he stood in the doorway and turned the wheel once with his thumb, watching it catch and hold the light.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, attacked the Marxist social interpretation.
story:
Adam had commandeer the last study carrel by the window, which meant he had arrived before Heather for the first time in the history of their friendship, and he intended to enjoy it. He spread his notes across the whole desk like a general claiming territory: six printouts, a battered copy of Rudé's The Crowd in the French Revolution, and an index card on which he had written, in increasingly desperate handwriting, "the moment when historians first seriously challenged the Marxist view???"

Ms. Goh had assigned the historiographical essay three weeks ago, and for three weeks Adam had understood nothing except that he was supposed to write about how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, not about the Revolution itself. "You are studying the historians, not the history," she had said, and then, ruinously, "It's historiography, the history of history," and half the class had made the sound people make when a word has too many syllables.

Heather dropped her bag on the floor beside him and pulled a granola bar from her coat, breaking it in half before he could ask. She did that. He took his half and tried not to look grateful, because they had an agreement about not being sappy, and gratitude of the visible kind counted as sappy.

"You still don't have your pivot," she said, chewing.

"I have everything except my pivot." He tapped the printouts. "Nineteenth century, everybody loves the Revolution, it's the birth of the modern world. Then the Marxists, and they own it for like fifty years, the bourgeoisie rising up, the whole class struggle thing. And then," and here he gestured at empty air, where his essay's second half presumably floated, "and then nothing. My notes just say 'somebody disagrees, somehow, at some point.'"

"Somebody always disagrees. That's the entire job."

Heather slid the sixth printout toward herself, the one he'd skimmed and given up on because the prose was dense and the author kept saying "so-called." She read the way she read, fast and unimpressed, and then she stopped being unimpressed. "Adam. This is your guy."

He leaned over. The printout was an old journal article, and buried in its second paragraph was a sentence about Alfred Cobban's 1954 inaugural lecture at University College London, published in 1955 as The Myth of the French Revolution, a lecture that had attacked the Marxist social interpretation. Adam read it twice. 1954, the lecture; 1955, the pamphlet. A man standing up at his own inaugural, in front of presumably many Marxists, and telling them the story they'd built was a myth. It was almost rude. It was perfect.

"That's the moment," Adam said. "That's the exact moment. Cobban, 1954, published 1955, The Myth of the French Revolution. He attacked the Marxist social interpretation right there, in his inaugural lecture, like a mic drop with footnotes." He wrote it on the index card and underlined it so hard the pen went through.

From Heather's side of the table, the afternoon looked different than it had an hour ago. She could see Adam's whole posture change, the hunch going out of his shoulders, and she thought, not for the first time, that he was easier to help than most people because he never pretended he didn't need it. She also noticed the boy two carrels over, the one who'd been circling the printer since fourth period, hovering near their desk now with the particular stillness of someone who wanted to ask something and couldn't. She recognized him. Maximiliano, from her chemistry class, who had once lent her a calculator during a fire drill and never asked for it back.

"You need the printer?" she asked him.

"I need," Maximiliano said carefully, "a book about the French Revolution that is not checked out. I checked. They are all checked out. Mostly by him." He pointed at Adam's stack.

Adam looked at Rudé's The Crowd in the French Revolution, which he had checked out mostly to feel official, and which he had not opened since Tuesday. There was a small war inside him, brief and atavistic, the ancient instinct of a sixteen-year-old hoarding resources at finals time. He lost it, which was the good outcome.

"You can take Rudé if you want," he said, pushing it across. "I'm not really using it. Honestly I'm writing about historians arguing with each other, which is like the Revolution but with more passive aggression." Maximiliano took the book with the solemnity of someone receiving a kidney, and Adam watched him go, then looked at his index card again, Cobban, 1954, 1955, and realized the essay had a shape now: love, then class struggle, then a man in a lecture hall saying no, and a hundred years of historians arguing about whether he was right. He did not know yet what he thought about Cobban himself, whether the attack had been fair or just fashionable, and he suspected Ms. Goh would ask exactly that, and he suspected the honest answer was that he was still figuring it out, and that maybe that was allowed.

Heather reached over and stole the last inch of her own granola bar back off his paper.

"Outline by Friday," she said. "I'll read it if you read mine."

"Deal," said Adam, and turned to a clean page.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A home with a 1 percent yearly flood chance has about a 26 percent chance of flooding at least once during a 30-year mortgage.
story:
The trail climbed out of the parking lot through a stand of boreal spruce, dark and resinous, and Alexis carried his mother's old tablet in a padded sleeve against his chest like something that might bruise. Ms. Hughes had promised them one bar of signal at the lookout, one window to upload their finished map layers before the state GIS competition closed at five o'clock. It was ten past three. He had the floodplain data cached, the census housing layer cached, everything cached, but no way to know whether his overlay would render until it reached a server somewhere.

"Slow down," Nancy called behind him. "Some of us didn't sleep in a lab."

He hadn't slept in a lab. He'd slept at the kitchen table with his chin on his forearms, rerunning the numbers on Mr. Renner's new house. Mr. Renner had bought near the river in the spring and called it a bargain, and Alexis, wanting a real test case for his project, had looked up the parcel's rating. One percent yearly flood chance. It had sounded like nothing. Then he'd done the arithmetic across a thirty-year mortgage, since that was how long Mr. Renner would be paying, and the answer had come out at roughly twenty-six percent, and he had sat very still in the dark kitchen, because a one-in-four shot at the river coming in was not what a bargain meant to him anymore.

Drayden caught up at the switchback, breathing hard, smelling of the orange he'd peeled at the trailhead. "So your map's going to win," he said, not quite a question.

"It overlays flood risk on housing values. Nobody else is doing both layers."

"Because it's depressing?"

"Because it's true." Nancy said it before Alexis could, and the way she said it made him glance at her, but she was watching the slope ahead, where Ms. Hughes had stopped and turned around, wind moving the collar of her jacket.

"Checkpoint," Ms. Hughes said. "Everyone's file uploaded and verified before I let anyone on the bus home. That's the deadline, not five o'clock. Five o'clock is the state's deadline. Mine is the lookout." She smiled as she said it, but nobody smiled back.

They climbed. The spruce gave way to granite and low blueberry scrub, and Alexis's calves burned and his mind kept running the overlay anyway, the way it had all week. At school the problem had been abstract, two colored layers and a legend. At home it had become one gray-shingled house with a porch swing, and that was the part he hadn't told anyone yet, not Nancy, not Drayden, not even his mother, who had stood behind his chair on Thursday night with her hand resting on the back of it. He had minimized the window fast, and she had asked what he was hiding, and he had said homework. The veracity of that was thin and they both knew it. He hadn't lied, exactly. He had only withheld.

The lookout opened all at once, wind and light and the whole valley laid out below them, the river a bright slack ribbon through the middle of town. Alexis sat on the leeward side of a boulder, dug out the tablet, and watched the signal icon flicker from nothing to one thin bar. His upload box appeared. Behind him he heard Drayden say, "Renner's place is out past the second bend, right? My dad delivers gravel out there," and Alexis's thumb stopped above the button.

"Who's Renner?" Nancy asked, coming around the boulder with her own phone raised, hunting her own signal.

"Family friend. Just bought a house by the river." Alexis kept his eyes on the screen. "One percent chance of flooding any given year. Sounds safe."

Drayden shrugged. "One in a hundred. I'd take those odds."

"Over thirty years, though. Over a whole mortgage, it's about a twenty-six percent chance it floods at least once."

Nancy lowered her phone. Out on the slope the wind came up again, carrying the smell of cold stone, and for a moment nobody said anything, and Alexis understood that they were all doing the same arithmetic he had done alone in the kitchen, and that it changed the color of the valley below, the ribbon of the river, the little roofs along its banks.

"So the map," Nancy said slowly. "The dark red parcels."

"Somebody lives in all of them." He had built the project to prove a point about the whole city, and somewhere between Thursday night and this granite ledge the point had narrowed to one swing on one porch, and he did not yet know whether to go tell Mr. Renner, or whether a sixteen-year-old with a cached dataset had any business walking up to a man's new driveway with numbers. Maybe the models were coarse. Maybe the parcel boundary was off by fifty feet. He could feel both things being true at once, the risk and the uncertainty inside the risk, and he could not flatten either one into a clean conclusion.

"Four fifteen," Ms. Hughes called. "Verification emails are coming through. Alexis?"

The upload bar crawled, stuck at ninety-one percent, the signal icon guttering. Nancy crouched beside him without touching the tablet, her shadow falling across it, and Drayden stood a little way off with his hands in his pockets, looking down the valley toward the second bend where the roofs were.

"Ninety-four," Nancy said quietly.

The wind shifted. The bar crossed to ninety-nine, hung there long enough that Alexis heard his own pulse, and then the screen flashed to the confirmation page, his two layers merged, the town rendered in blue and red, finished, submitted, unchangeable until morning.

He stood up and looked down at the river.

"I'm going to Renner's tonight," he said. "After the bus."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
The lunch rush had emptied out of Casa Marina by two o'clock, leaving Rebecca with one occupied table, a pile of menus to restack, and the newspaper someone had left wedged behind the salt shaker. It was a Spanish daily, days old, creased down the middle. She had been in the country's kitchen of the language for three years of high school classes and could order food and describe the weather, but she had never once read a real article, and Ms. Ramos, her old teacher, had said at graduation that the gap between textbook Spanish and newspaper Spanish was the gap between a swimming pool and the sea.

"¿Puedo ver eso?" Sebastien asked from the counter, or something like that; he worked the register on Saturdays and had been born into the language the way she had been born into English, without effort or merit. He reached for the paper, and she pulled it back against her apron.

"I'm reading it," she said. "Out loud. To you. And then I have to summarize it, in Spanish, in my own words." She had promised her grandmother she would try. Her grandmother had come to this city with nothing, had spent decades as a seamstress and then, destitute after the shop closed, had started over cleaning offices at sixty-two, and the only inheritance she talked about was the language itself, which she said Rebecca had let leak out of her like air from a cheap tire.

Rebecca smoothed the article flat and began. "El gobierno anunció... el gobierno anunció una nueva política..." Sebastien winced at her vowels the way a person winces at a flat note, and she kept going anyway, word by word, the sentences assembling themselves slowly, like furniture with too many parts. Then she hit a line that stopped her: the government, the article said, had declared that the new amnesty would cover ten thousand families. She looked up. "Is that true? Did it cover them?"

"Read the whole sentence," Sebastien said. She read it again. Según una fuente del ministerio, la amnistía cubrirá a diez mil familias. "Según," he said, tapping the word. "According to." She stared at the little word. The sentence had seemed like a wall of identical bricks, and suddenly one brick was a door. The reporter was not telling her ten thousand families would be covered; the reporter was telling her that someone at the ministry said so, and those were two different things entirely. The claim had a signature on it. She had spent a whole semester in Rory's civics class listening to him historicize every headline, dragging each one back to its era and its interests until she wanted to scream that sometimes a fact was just a fact, and here was the same lesson arriving in a second language, more gently, folded inside a single word.

She remembered ninth grade, actually, before any of this: Rory sliding into the seat beside her at the pizza place near school, holding up his phone with a headline about some study, saying, "Watch, I bet it says 'studies show,' which means nobody shows anything." She had rolled her eyes so hard she'd nearly seen her own brain. But she'd also underlined "studies show" in her notebook that night, secretly, which felt now like planting a seed and then forgetting which pot it was in.

"Okay," she said, and turned back to Sebastien. "Entonces, la noticia dice que, según el ministerio, la amnistía..." She stumbled through it, hands moving as if she could shape the summary in the air. "The article says that, according to the ministry, the amnesty will cover ten thousand families. But the reporter doesn't say it will happen. The reporter says the ministry says it." She grinned, unable to stop it. "I have been scared of this newspaper for twenty minutes and it turns out it's mostly just people quoting each other."

Sebastien laughed, that short exhale he used instead of actual laughing, and told her that was more or less what his mother said about all journalism, though with more cursing. He made her read the next paragraph, and the next, and the third one gave her trouble, a verb form she could not untangle, and she had to admit she did not know whether the mayor had promised housing or merely announced an intention to study the problem of housing. That part stayed murky. She could hold the según in her hand, but the rest of the language was still a sea, and she was still swimming in it with her shoes on.

Ms. Ramos came in at three, as she did every Saturday for the fish soup, and found Rebecca at the corner table with the newspaper spread out and her phone showing a translation app she was no longer consulting. "You look like a woman with news," Ms. Ramos said, sitting down without being asked.

"Según the ministry," Rebecca said, pointing at the sentence, "ten thousand families. But I'm only reporting the source. I'm not vouching for it." Ms. Ramos raised an eyebrow, and Rebecca sat up straight, cleared her throat, and began again, this time out loud, in Spanish, from the top of the article, while Sebastien leaned on the counter and winced at every vowel.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The US Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996 gives food donors limited protection from liability, which encourages stores and restaurants to donate surplus food.
story:
Eve had signed up for the neighborhood cleanup because Amber said it would look good on applications, and she had ended up, by some failure of the sorting process, inside the food bank on Carden Street, taping labels onto shelves while everyone else raked the lot outside. The building smelled of cardboard and disinfectant. Behind her, a woman in a flour-dusted apron carried in two paper sacks and set them on the counter as though they might detonate.

"I don't know if you can even take these," the woman said. "It's the bread from yesterday. My sister says if somebody gets sick, they sue you, and I lose the bakery. But it seems wrong to throw it out." She was small, decisive, the kind of person who apologized with her chin rather than her voice. Mr. Levy, who ran the place and had introduced himself to Eve an hour earlier with a firm handshake and a list of instructions, looked at the sacks and then at his clipboard, and Eve could see him doing arithmetic that had nothing to do with flour.

Eve's mother had a theory about these things. Her mother believed that giving away food was bad business dressed up as goodness, that people took kindness and expected it forever, and that the woman with the bakery was right to worry. Eve had grown up fluent in this theory the way you grow up fluent in a household language, and she had signed up for the cleanup partly to test whether she believed any of it. Outside the window, Ahmed was dragging a broken crate toward the dumpster, pausing to read its faded label as if the crate were a document in a case he was building.

"We can't turn away food," Mr. Levy said, but he said it without conviction, which was its own kind of information. "We just have to be careful. I'd have to call somebody." The baker pulled her keys from her apron, jingling them, halfway to leaving, and Eve felt the whole exchange tipping toward the dumpster and the raccoons and the wrongness the woman herself had named. So she took out her phone. It felt rude, standing there in front of adults, but she typed it anyway: can a bakery donate leftover bread without getting sued.

The answer came up fast, which surprised her, the way true things that have been waiting a long time surprise you. There was a federal law, the Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act of 1996. It gave people who donated food limited protection from liability, and the article she found said that this was exactly why stores and restaurants felt safe donating their surplus. She read it twice, because she wanted to be sure before she said anything. She knew how easy it was to hand somebody a wrong fact with total confidence, and she did not want to be the person who cost a bakery its business with a sentence.

"There's a law," she said, and both adults turned, and she made herself keep going, phone held out. "The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act. From 1996. It gives food donors limited protection from liability." The words came out in the wrong rhythm, like a recitation, but she could not find a smoother way to say a legal sentence. "That's why stores and restaurants donate their surplus. It's the whole point of the law."

Mr. Levy took the phone. He read with his lips moving slightly, which Eve found oddly comforting, since it meant he was actually reading. The baker watched his face the way people watch a scale settle. "I've heard of it," he said finally. "I never looked at it directly." He handed the phone back and, in the same motion, pulled the sacks toward him and began counting the loaves, and something in his posture changed, some gate opening. The baker exhaled through her nose, once, and started untying her apron as though she had been wearing it as armor.

"You learn something every day," she said, and then, to Eve, "You're not one of his regulars, are you? I've never seen you." Eve explained the cleanup, the mix-up, Amber and the applications, and heard how thin it sounded, as though she had wandered in off the street. Which, in a sense, she had. The baker said she would come back Thursday with the leftover rolls from the weekend, and Thursday after that, and Eve realized she was watching the creation of a habit, a small civic machinery assembling itself around two sacks of yesterday's bread.

Amber came in at noon to find her, cheeks pink from raking, and asked what she'd done all morning, and Eve found she could not compress it into anything Amber would find interesting. "Shelved cans. Looked something up." Ahmed trailed in behind her, carrying the broken crate, which he had decided could hold the rolled oats if they turned it right side up. Mr. Levy accepted the crate with the grave courtesy of a man being converted to another's idea, and Eve thought about her mother's theory again, testing it against the morning. Her mother was not entirely wrong; the bakery could not give away everything, and goodness did run on arithmetic as much as on bread. But the fear had been the larger number in that equation, and the law had changed the arithmetic, and that was something her mother's theory had never accounted for: that people wanted to do the right thing and mostly needed to know it was safe.

She was honest with herself about what stayed uncertain. She did not know whether Thursday's rolls would actually arrive, or whether the baker's sister would call with some counter-argument Eve hadn't found, or whether a law that protected donors also protected the people eating day-old bread in every way that mattered. Amber was already pulling her toward the door, saying the pizza place on the corner had donated extra pies to the volunteers and it was first come first served. Eve followed her out into the lot, where the rakes stood upright against the fence like an honor guard, or like acolytes, she thought, though she wasn't sure of the word until she'd thought it. The pizza was greasy and extravagant and, after a morning of other people's hunger, almost hedonistic, and she ate her slice slowly while Amber recounted the morning's drama of the stolen rake. Eve listened, and watched Ahmed carry his crate of oats to the shelf, and decided she would come back on Thursday, just to see.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Carryover cooking means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast's internal temperature can rise by several degrees while it rests.
story:
Oliver's mother had left the roast on the bottom shelf of the refrigerator with a note taped to the plastic wrap: "Dinner at 7, if you feel brave." She was covering the late shift at the hospital, his father was two states away at a conference, and for the first time in his seventeen years the Sunday meal was his alone. He had the recipe open on Ms. Ito's old kitchen thermometer, borrowed that afternoon from next door, and he had read the same sentence six times: remove the roast at an internal temperature of 135 degrees for medium rare.

He set the probe at half past five, calculated backward from the cooking time, and slid the pan into the oven. Steven had texted him a photo of a parking lot and the words "we're early, save us a slice," and Mariane had sent a longer message about how her own family's dinners had gone silent since her brother left for college, how she missed even the arguments. Oliver answered her while the fat began to crackle, then put the phone face down because the numbers on the thermometer were climbing faster than the recipe promised, and he wanted to watch.

At 6:40 the probe read 131. He decided he would not wait for 135; the roast would sit, the pan would sit, everything would hold its temperature, and the margin would protect him. At 6:52 it read 135 exactly and he pulled the pan out, tented it with foil the way his mother did, and felt the small pride of a plan obeyed. He called Ms. Ito because she had told him to let her know how it went, and because she was the only adult on the street whose voice didn't make him feel eleven years old.

"It's at 135," he said. "It's resting now."

"Pull it out earlier next time," she said. "It's called carryover cooking. The food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a big roast like that can rise several degrees while it rests."

He stood holding the phone, looking at the foil, and understood that his margin had been an illusion, that he had aimed at the finish line instead of the space before it. Ms. Ito hadn't scolded him; she had simply handed him the fact and let him do the arithmetic himself. He thanked her, hung up, and did the arithmetic: 135 plus several degrees put him well past medium rare, somewhere in the territory his father called "punishment meat," said with a dour face that Oliver had always found funnier than his father intended.

When he cut into it at 7:10, the center was the rosy brown of medium, edible and even good, but not what he'd been aiming at. Mariane and Steven arrived with paper cups of soda and no commentary, which was its own kind of commentary. "It's actually delicious," Mariane said, and Steven, chewing, said, "This is like when you tell me the bus is coming and it's already coming." Oliver laughed, then stopped laughing, because the roast had cost him something and he wanted to sit with the cost for a minute instead of covering it.

Between bites he told them about carryover cooking, and Mariane said that most of the good advice she'd ever gotten worked like that, arriving a moment too late to be useful and exactly on time to be remembered. Steven argued, mouth full, that late advice was still advice, that he'd rather know the thing for next time than never know it, and Oliver found himself changing his own position mid-argument: he had started the meal believing that precision meant hitting the number, and now he believed precision meant understanding what happened after the number, which felt less like control and more like respect. He couldn't fully explain the difference, and said so, and Mariane said that not being able to explain something was not the same as being wrong about it, which was either profound or an oxymoron, depending on how tired you were.

They left him the last slice because he had cooked it, an old rule of his mother's that had survived her absence. He wrapped the bone and the slice in foil and set it in the refrigerator with a new note in his own handwriting, one he planned to leave where his mother would find it on her break: "Pulled it at 135, it kept going, next time I'll aim lower. Also, Mariane says hi." It wasn't an apology and it wasn't a triumph; it was a record of a thing learned the only way he ever seemed to learn anything, slightly too late for the roast and just in time for everything after it.

He washed the pan in the quiet kitchen, steam rising off the water, and through the window Ms. Ito's porch light came on across the yard, a small yellow square in the dark.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
story:
Andrew had made the quarterfinals in Lincoln-Douglas, which meant two hours to kill before the round, and he had promised Darcy and Kassandra a rehearsal for the one-act he was directing, so he carried his debate tub and a spiral of blocking notes into an empty classroom on the second floor of the tournament school and pushed the desks against the wall. The fluorescent lights hummed. Somewhere below, a parliamentarian was reading pairings over the loudspeaker, and Andrew felt the double life he was leading this weekend press on him from both sides, the resolutions about jurisprudence waiting in his tub, the play waiting in his hands.

"We only have until your round," Kassandra said, dropping her bag by the radiator. She had the lead role, a girl who keeps a lighthouse lit for a brother she pretends is still at sea. Darcy played the brother, which meant he spent most of the play not there, and the rest of it arriving.

They ran the second scene, the one where the brother crosses the stage twice, and the first time it happened Andrew stopped them. Every time Darcy walked from the door to the table, he ended up standing directly in front of Kassandra, and from where Andrew sat in the fifth row of desks, she vanished. He could hear her voice coming out of Darcy's shoulder. "Hold on," he said, and walked up onto the stage area they had marked with tape, and stood where Kassandra had been standing, and had Darcy cross again, and it was true, he lost her completely.

"Can I just move further upstage?" Kassandra asked. She shifted back toward the wall, but the light up there was flat and gray, and when Darcy crossed again she was still half-eaten by his shadow, and now she looked stranded, like a person standing at the edge of a photograph. Darcy apologized twice, tried crossing faster, tried crossing on a different diagonal, and nothing helped; the stage seemed to belong to whoever was moving across it, and whoever stood still got buried.

Andrew sat on a desk and looked at his notes, at the little arrows he had drawn, arrows that had seemed so decisive at his kitchen table and now meant nothing. In debate he would have solved this the way he solved everything, by finding the flaw in the opposing case, but there was no opposing case, only two people and a bad arrangement of space. He thought about how his coach, Mr. Shapiro, kept telling him his closing speeches were all argument and no weight, that he positioned ideas the way a bad director positioned actors, one in front of the other so the audience only ever saw one thing at a time. He had filed the comment away as obsolescent, one of those phrases adults reused until it went soft. Now he unfiled it.

"Go back to where you were," he said to Kassandra. "Downstage, where the light's good. And Darcy, when you cross to the table, I want you to cross, and then I want her to move." He walked it himself first, Darcy's path, and then took Kassandra's place, and after the cross he shifted a half-step toward the door, opening the space, and from the desks he could see them both at once, separate and balanced, neither one hiding the other. "Like that. You shift to balance him. You counter the cross."

They ran it. Darcy crossed, Kassandra countered, and suddenly the scene looked like something, like two people in a real room negotiating over invisible territory. Kassandra grinned at him, and Darcy, who apologized for everything, apologized for nothing. Mr. Shapiro, who had come up to tell Andrew the quarterfinal pairings were posted, stood in the doorway for a minute with his arms folded, watching the next cross and the answering shift. "Nice countering," he said, and pointed at Andrew. "Room two-oh-four, in ten minutes. Opponent's from Hale."

Andrew checked his watch. The dress rehearsal for the one-act was Sunday afternoon, the same hour as finals if he kept winning, and he had assumed all along, without ever saying it aloud, that he would choose the debate, because debate was the thing he was good at and directing was the thing he was trying on. But watching Darcy and Kassandra run the scene again, countering each other in the gray light, he felt something he did not feel in rounds, something that made the back of his neck hot and his hands useless, an exhilaration that had nothing to do with winning.

"Run it twice more," he said, picking up his tub. "Kassandra, when he crosses the second time, counter downstage instead of up, and we'll see which reads better from the back." He paused at the door. "If I make finals, Darcy takes notes." Darcy looked up, surprised, and Kassandra laughed and said, "He's changing, he's actually changing," and Andrew went down the stairs two at a time toward room two-oh-four.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
story:
Arianna had never been inside her grandmother's house when it was this full. Relatives stood in the kitchen holding paper plates they didn't eat from, and someone had covered the hallway mirror with a grey sheet, and her mother sat on a low wooden stool near the window, her regular chair pushed aside. The burial had been that morning. Arianna kept her coat on because taking it off felt like agreeing to stay, and staying meant admitting the house now belonged to a dead woman.

She had planned to be somewhere else. She'd told her mother she might go to Sarah-Maude's, that she had a chem assignment, and her mother had said fine in a flat, noncommittal voice that made Arianna feel worse than an argument would have. Instead she'd sat in the driveway for twenty minutes with the engine off, and then come inside anyway.

"Larry's outside," her cousin reported, hovering by the door with his shoes still on. "He wants to know if he can come in or if it's family only." Arianna went out to the porch. Larry stood at the bottom of the steps holding a foil pan of something, the way you might arrive at a potluck, and she saw at once that he had no idea what he was walking into. Neither, honestly, did she. Her grandmother had been the religious one, in her quiet way, and Arianna had absorbed almost nothing of it except the smell of Friday candles and a grandmotherly rationalism about everything else, a firm belief that most problems yielded to logic and a good night's sleep. Death had not yielded to either.

"Come in," she said. "It's called shiva. It means seven, and that's how many days we sit, after the burial." Larry looked at the foil pan. "My mom sent kugel," he said. "Is that wrong?" "Nothing's wrong," she said, and found she almost meant it. "There are casseroles on every surface. One more won't extenuate anything." She wasn't sure that was the right word until it was out, and Larry laughed, which surprised them both.

Inside, Sarah-Maude arrived next, empty-handed and embarrassed about it, whispering that she'd googled what to bring and gotten ten contradictory answers. Arianna walked her to the kitchen, poured her tea she didn't ask for, and stood with her while Sarah-Maude asked, in a low voice, what she was supposed to say to Arianna's mother. "You don't have to say anything good," Arianna told her. "There isn't a right sentence. People keep trying to find one and then not coming over at all, which is worse." She watched Sarah-Maude absorb this, watched her cross the room and sit on the carpet beside the low stool, saying nothing, just being a warm body near her mother, and watched her mother reach down and grip Sarah-Maude's sleeve like a rope.

The afternoon went on like that. Arianna learned the shape of the week from the relatives themselves, from the uncles who said they'd be back tomorrow and the day after, from a great-aunt who counted the days off on her fingers, seven of them, starting only now that the burial was done. Nobody lectured her. She pieced it together the way she'd pieced together the layout of the house as a child, room by room, and by evening she understood that the low stool and the covered mirror and the kugel were all parts of one sentence everyone was saying with their bodies: we do not rush this.

Near dusk she went upstairs to her grandmother's room, the one place the crowd hadn't reached. The bed was still unmade from the last hospital-adjacent week, and on the nightstand lay the grandmother's reading glasses and a paperback about Jewish history with a receipt marking a page. Arianna picked it up and sat on the edge of the mattress. Downstairs someone had started singing, badly, and her mother's voice joined in anyway.

She had come here to say goodbye to her grandmother, and she had been dreading it all week, rehearsing a quiet moment at the bedside that would hurt the right amount and then be over. Instead she was the one being looked after. When she finally came down, her mother abandoned her circle of cousins, crossed the whole crowded room, took Arianna's face in both hands, and said, "You ate nothing today. Sit. I'll fix you a plate." Then she went to the kitchen, took the kugel Larry's mother had sent, cut the first piece, and set it in front of her daughter.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: Winston Churchill said in a speech at Fulton, Missouri, on March 5, 1946, that an iron curtain had descended across Europe.
story:
Hunter had reserved the study room at the public library for two hours, and he had forty minutes left, which was not enough time to decide who was right. He had two books open on the table, one by a historian who blamed the Soviet Union for the Cold War, one by a historian who blamed the United States. Both of them quoted the same speech, and that was the problem.

The speech was the one where Winston Churchill said an iron curtain had descended across Europe. Hunter had read that line a dozen times before he noticed something. He checked the copyright page, then the index, then the notes at the back, and found what he was looking for: the speech had been delivered at Fulton, Missouri, on March 5, 1946. Missouri. He sat back and looked at the ceiling tiles for a while, because the detail rearranged something in his head, though he could not yet say what.

He texted Elsie, who was two tables away in the main room, pretending to study for chemistry. She came in without knocking, dropped into the chair across from him, and stole one of his pretzels. "You realize it's spring break," she said.

"Churchill gave that speech in Fulton, Missouri," Hunter said. "March 5, 1946." He turned the book so she could see the footnote. "Not in London. Not in Parliament. In Missouri, to a small college audience, with Truman sitting there."

Elsie chewed the pretzel and looked at him the way she looked at most of his historical discoveries, fondly and with mild impatience. "And this matters because?"

"Because the first book uses it as proof the Soviets were already sealing off Europe. The second book uses it as proof the Americans were already campaigning against the Soviets, so obviously Moscow got nervous." He tapped each cover in turn. "Same words. Different crime."

Outside the study room's glass wall, the afternoon light had gone long and yellow across the carpet. Somewhere near the front desk a printer ground through somebody's tax forms. Elsie said the line was still the line, wherever it was said; a curtain was a curtain. Hunter said that was exactly the kind of thinking that got people writing five-paragraph essays with a thesis and no evidence, and she said that was the kind of thinking that got people forty minutes from a deadline and no thesis at all, and they were both right, which was the annoying thing.

He pulled the two books toward him again and tried it a different way. Not which historian was right, but what each one would have to admit for the other to be right. The first would have to concede that a speech given in Missouri, to an American audience, with the American president presiding, was itself an act, a move in the game, not just a description of one. The second would have to concede that a curtain could descend without anyone in Missouri asking it to. Hunter wrote both sentences in his notebook, then looked at them. The reverie lasted until he noticed he had been holding his pen without writing anything for several minutes, and Elsie had left and come back with a book about Viking ships.

Hashim arrived at four with his backpack still smelling faintly of the coffee shop where he worked mornings. He was the one who had started the whole argument, sort of, by eulogizing the second historian in class two weeks ago, calling him the last honest man in the field, and Ms. Somsak had said, in that dry way of hers, that Hunter might try reading somebody who disagreed before he agreed with anybody. Hunter still wasn't sure whether that had been advice or an assignment.

Hashim sat down, read Hunter's two sentences, and pushed the notebook back. "You're not answering the question. The question is who started it."

"The question might be bad," Hunter said. "The speech exists. The date exists. March 5, 1946, Fulton, Missouri. After that, both books are just choosing which half of the room to stand in." He heard how that sounded, like he was claiming a sophistication he hadn't earned, and it embarrassed him a little, because the truth was he still didn't know. What he had was a location, a date, and the uneasy sense that evidence didn't settle arguments so much as show you where the arguing actually began.

Ms. Somsak passed the study room on her way to the returns cart, her arms full of held books, and slowed when she saw the three of them bent over the table. She looked at the open pages, at Hunter's notebook, at the putative outline he had written at the top of the page and then crossed out. She didn't come in. She just nodded once, the way people nod at a project they decide not to interrupt, and continued down the aisle toward biography.

Hunter turned to a blank page. "Okay," he said, and clicked his pen twice. "New thesis. The curtain was real, and so was the stage it was announced on." He wrote it down before he could talk himself out of it, and Elsie, leaning over to read it upside down, stole another pretzel.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate, the direction a positive charge would be pushed.
story:
The skate park at five in the afternoon turned the color of weak tea, the light coming through the fence jaundiced and low, and Elizabeth sat on the flat bottom of the bowl with a binder on her knees and a pencil she had already chewed through. The exam was at eight the next morning. Ms. Pérez had said, on her way out of sixth period, that the field problems would be half the points, and Elizabeth had nodded as though she understood, which she had not, entirely.

"Twenty minutes," Zane said, rolling past. "Then I need the bowl for the line. Contest submission closes at midnight and I don't have the clip yet." He dropped in, missed, and climbed out swearing at the coping, which was scuffed like something out of antiquity, a surface that generations of wheels had worn down before his.

Ruth sat cross-legged beside Elizabeth with her own binder open, though hers was mostly a copy of Elizabeth's, made at lunch in a hurry. "I can't stay past six," Ruth said. "My shift starts at six thirty, and my mom's already mad about last week." She tapped the page. "So settle this before I go. Which way do the arrows go? For the plates."

Elizabeth looked down at her diagram. Two parallel lines, a positive plate and a negative plate, arrows drawn neatly between them pointing from the negative toward the positive. She had drawn it two nights ago while half watching a lecture video, and it had looked so reasonable since that she had stopped questioning it. She had spent that same evening titrating a solution for chemistry, adding drops until the color changed, and she remembered how sure she had been right up until the moment the indicator proved her wrong. That memory made her hesitate now, pencil hovering.

"Mine says that way," she said slowly. "From negative to positive."

"So does mine," Ruth said. "I copied it off you."

Zane rolled to a stop beside them, board ticking against the concrete. He leaned over, breathing hard, sweat darkening the collar of his shirt. "That's backwards," he said.

"You failed this unit," Ruth said.

"I failed the test. The unit I failed beautifully, and I paid for it in summer school, thank you." He crouched and put his finger on the positive plate. "Okay. Field between two charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate. That's the direction a positive charge would be pushed. Like the drop-in. You start up here and everything pushes you down. You don't start at the bottom and get pushed up."

Elizabeth turned her pencil around and erased her arrows, all six of them, until the paper was smudged gray. She redrew them pointing the other way, from positive to negative, from the plate marked plus toward the plate marked minus, the way a proton, if you set one loose in there, would actually travel. It was strange how the corrected picture looked less intuitive than the wrong one, and she sat with that for a second. She still couldn't say why the field went that way, only that it did, and she was honest enough with herself to mark a small star beside the diagram meaning ask Ms. Pérez tomorrow, before the exam, not during it.

"Fix mine too," Ruth said, already flipping to her own page, holding out the binder like an offering. "If I fail this I lose the parking spot my dad promised me, and he's been holding that over me since September."

Elizabeth copied the arrows across. Ruth checked her phone, swore softly, stood, gathered her things. "Six oh two. I'm dead. Text me if you figure out the series circuit one." She left her half-finished energy drink as payment, which was the custom between them, and jogged toward the gate.

Zane dropped back into the bowl, pushed twice, and carved a long line along the transition, his wheels singing against the concrete in the dying light. Elizabeth watched him set up for the trick, the one he'd been failing for an hour, the one the midnight deadline hinged on. She looked down at her diagram, at the little arrows now pointing the way they should, then up at the sky gone orange above the fence.

He landed it. Clean, silent for a half second, then the clatter of the tail and the roll-out, and he looked up at her grinning like the whole day had been rigged in his favor from the start.

"See," he called. "Positive to negative. Everything rolls downhill."

"You still failed the test," she called back, and closed her binder on the smudged page.

activity: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
knowledge_domain: to weigh two historians' differing explanations of the Cold War against the evidence
fact: William Appleman Williams's 1959 book The Tragedy of American Diplomacy began the revisionist school, arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War.
story:
Victor found the book on his grandfather's shelf between a water-stained atlas and a box of fishing leaders, wedged in so tightly he had to work it loose with two fingers. The Tragedy of American Diplomacy, by William Appleman Williams, 1959. He had come out to the house for a quiet weekend to finish his history paper, and the quiet had already gone wrong twice: once when the screen door shrieked, once when his phone buzzed with Alison's message, "did you pick traditionalist or revisionist, I said traditionalist, easier to defend." Victor sat down on the braided rug with the book and opened it to a random page and read a sentence that made him stop chewing the inside of his cheek.

The author was American. That was the part Victor had to read three times, because in class Mr. Novák had laid out the old debate on the whiteboard, the orthodox view that Soviet aggression started the Cold War and the revisionist view that blamed the West, and Victor had assumed the revisionists were, what, defectors, cranks, people with an ax to grind. But here was an American professor arguing that American economic expansion helped cause the Cold War, and the copyright page said the book had begun the whole revisionist school. Victor texted Ines, who was doing the same paper: "williams was american and still blamed the US. 1959. tragedy of american diplomacy." Her reply came back fast: "so? plenty of americans criticize america." He typed and deleted two answers before giving up and going to find his grandfather.

The old man was in the kitchen peeling apples in one long spiral, the peels curling into the sink, the fruit smelling sharp and green. "Grandpa, this book of yours. You read it?" His grandfather squinted at the cover, then at Victor, and said he'd read it in 1962, the year he came to this country. "Your teacher," he said, which was how he always referred to Mr. Novák, though the two had never met, "he is Czech?" Victor said yes. "Then ask him who gave him his framework." He went back to the apples, and the knife made its small even sound against the skin, and Victor understood that this was all he would get.

He took the book out to the porch, where the afternoon sun had heated the boards through his jeans, and a wasp investigated his soda can with bureaucratic patience.
