He made two columns in his notebook, the way Mr. Novák had shown them: explanation on one side, evidence on the other. Williams said economic expansion; on the other side Victor wrote what he actually knew from the documents they'd read in class, the Marshall Plan, the speeches, the satellite states. The problem, he was starting to see, was that the same evidence could sit under both columns like a cat that would sleep in either chair. He wrote "confounder?" next to the Marshall Plan and underlined it twice, and then felt foolish, and left it underlined anyway.

Alison called at five. "Ines says you found some book that changed your mind." "It didn't change my mind. It moved the question." He could hear her rolling her eyes through the phone. "Victor. The paper's due Tuesday. You can't write 'the question moved.'" He said he could write that both explanations were tenable if you were honest about what the documents couldn't settle, and she said "tenable" was a coward's word, and he said no, it was the only honest word, and she hung up in the way she hung up, which meant she was thinking about it.

The wasp was gone and the light had gone long and yellow when Mr. Novák's car, or a car exactly like it, turned out to be the car of the neighbor from three houses down, a man Victor's grandfather played chess with on Sundays. Not Mr. Novák, then, no rescue. Victor went back inside for dinner, and over the stew his grandfather asked what he had concluded. "I don't know yet," Victor said. "Williams makes a case. But a case isn't proof. And I keep wanting it to be proof, because it would be a better paper." His grandfather snorted into his bowl. "You want the argument to be good," he said, "or you want it to be true?" Victor said both, and his grandfather laughed for real, a sound like the screen door.

After dinner Victor sat at the kitchen table with the lamp on and the moths ticking against the window, and he wrote the paragraph he had been circling all day. He wrote that Williams's explanation accounted for the economic record and that the orthodox account accounted for the seizures of the satellite states, that both drew on real documents, and that what stayed uncertain was which weight to assign, because the evidence did not come labeled. He remembered his grandfather's word, framework, and added a sentence about how a framework decides what counts as evidence before the evidence arrives, which felt like the truest thing he'd written all year. He read it over and did not strike it out.

His phone buzzed. Alison: "fine. tenable. but you're buying my coffee monday." Victor set the phone face-down beside the notebook, closed Williams and squared him on the shelf between the atlas and the fishing leaders, and turned off the lamp.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: For Mexico's Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2, families build home altars called ofrendas with orange marigolds, whose bright color and strong scent are believed to guide souls home.
story:
The cultural center smelled of marigolds before Jackson even got through the doors, a dense sweetness that his mother said reminded her of her father's garden in Veracruz. This was the first year the center had held a Day of the Dead celebration for the whole town, not just the families who had kept the tradition quietly at home, and his mother had signed them up to build an altar in the main hall. She had been carrying his grandfather's photograph in her purse since September, wrapped in a paper towel, waiting for November.

The hall had been arranged with long tables along the walls, each one assigned to a family, and Jackson could see that some had gone far beyond photographs. There were sugar skulls with names piped across the foreheads in white icing, clay dishes of mole, tortillas stacked under cloth, and everywhere the orange marigolds, in bundles, in jars, their petals scattered along the table edges like a dropped trail. A woman from the center was explaining the schedule to a cluster of volunteers, and Jackson caught the word ofrenda as she gestured at the altars. "Ofrenda," she said, touching the edge of the nearest table, and the volunteers nodded and wrote it down.

His mother unpacked slowly, setting out pan de muerto she had baked that morning, a small glass of water, and the photograph, which she unwrapped and stood against a folded napkin. Jackson's job was the flowers. He had bought two bundles from the market on Friday, and now he began pulling off petals and laying them in a line from the door of the hall toward their table, which he had seen another family do, though he wasn't entirely sure why. It felt like guessing at a ritual he had only ever glimpsed over his grandfather's shoulder, years ago, in a house he mostly remembered as hot.

"You're making a path," said a voice behind him. Tristen was standing there with his hands in his pockets, holding a bundle of marigolds he seemed unsure what to do with. His family had come because Tristen's stepmother was from Oaxaca, and Tristen had told Jackson last week that he didn't really get it, that it seemed like a lot of effort for people who weren't there anymore. Jackson hadn't argued. He wasn't sure he got it either.

"The petals go from the entrance to the altar," Jackson said, mostly to sound like he knew. "Something about the smell." He said it with more confidence than he had, and Tristen crouched down and started dropping petals beside him, and for a while they worked in the noisy quiet of the hall, children running between tables, a musician tuning a guitar somewhere near the kitchen.

It was Mathilde who corrected him. She was at the next table arranging photographs in a careful row, four faces in what she called strict chronology, her great-grandparents in sequence, and she had overheard him without making a show of it. "It's not just the smell," she said, not unkindly, walking over. "The color too. The marigolds, the orange ones. Their bright color and strong scent are believed to guide the souls home. That's why the path." She glanced at his line of petals, then at the doorway. "You want it unbroken, I think. So nothing gets lost on the way in."

Jackson looked at his trail and saw the gaps, the places where he had been careless or distracted, and something in him flushed with the specific embarrassment of having performed a thing he didn't understand. But the feeling passed quickly, because Tristen was already filling in the gaps, kneeling on the tile, and because Jackson found he wanted to fix it more than he wanted to be right. The two of them worked backward from the altar to the door, thickening the line, and Jackson noticed his mother watching them from her chair with an expression he couldn't read, or could read only partially, which he suspected was the point of it.

Later, when the hall filled and the musician played songs his grandfather had liked, the volunteer woman passed near their table carrying trays of food for the communal supper, and Jackson overheard her telling someone that the days themselves mattered, that November first and second were when families did this, that it wasn't any random weekend but those two days, the first and the second of November. He filed that away, realizing he had never known it, that his mother's home altar had always just appeared in early November and he had never asked why those particular mornings. There was an epicurean table near the kitchen, heaped with candied pumpkin and hot chocolate, and he watched Tristen abandon his skepticism entirely for a plate of it, which made Jackson think that grief and appetite could share a table without any contradiction at all, that the whole evening was like that, two things true at once.

He still didn't know what he believed about souls finding their way along a path of petals. He knew the flowers were beautiful, and that his grandfather's face in the photograph looked younger than Jackson had ever known him, and that his mother had gone quiet in the way she did when she was holding something large. He went back to the doorway and stood there a moment, looking down the orange line to where his mother sat, then walked it slowly, the way a guest would, the way someone arriving home might.

Tristen looked up as Jackson reached the altar. "Good path," he said.

"Guided by an expert," Jackson said, and set one last marigold, whole and unbroken, beside the photograph.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: The US federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, though many states and cities set a higher minimum.
story:
Hunter filled out the application at the kitchen table on a Tuesday, pressing hard enough that the words showed through to the counter underneath. The store was called Rinaldi's, four blocks from his house, and the manager had told him they needed a bag boy for evenings and weekends. His mother read the form over his shoulder, said the schedule looked reasonable, and went back to the sink. He signed his name at the bottom the way he signed yearbooks, big and hurried.

They hired him that Friday. The manager, a saturnine man who moved through the aisles like he was auditing them, showed him where the bags were kept, thin and thick, and demonstrated a way of stacking cans that kept eggs from dying. Hunter practiced on a row of soup while a cashier watched without comment. He worked twelve hours that first week, mostly evenings, and on Thursday the manager handed him a thin envelope with his name printed on a stub inside.

He took the check home and laid it on the table under the lamp. $87.00. He did the arithmetic twice on the back of a water bill, and it came out the same both ways: seven dollars and twenty-five cents an hour. It was, as far as he knew, simply what jobs paid.

On Saturday, Dillon came over with his own check folded into quarters, and Reda arrived twenty minutes later with hers flat in a Ziploc bag, which she said was to keep it from getting bent. They spread all three on the table like evidence. Dillon's check, from a sandwich shop two towns over, was also for $7.25 an hour. Reda's was not.

"Hers is nine something," Dillon said. "Look. Per hour, right there." He tapped her stub with two fingers. Reda worked at a garden center just across the state line, a fifteen-minute drive her father made every morning on his way to the plant where he worked.

Reda said, "I didn't do anything. I didn't negotiate. I filled out a paper." She was as confused as they were, which somehow made it worse. Dillon, who had a tendency to treat every discrepancy as a personal insult, suggested that the garden center had made a clerical error in her favor and that she should keep quiet about it.

Hunter went upstairs and got his laptop. He typed the question plainly, why does my friend earn more per hour in the next state, and read for a while with his door open so he could hear them arguing below. What he found was this: the federal minimum wage had been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, and many states and cities set a higher minimum of their own. Rinaldi's paid the federal number. The garden center, across the line, paid what their state required, which was more.

He came back down and told them, reading the date off his phone to be sure he had it right. "Since July of 2009," he said. "That's the federal one. States can go above it." Dillon took the phone and scrolled, his mouth set, and then set it down without a word. The same country, the same kind of work, and a line on a map you could cross in fifteen minutes made the difference between seven twenty-five and nine something.

Dillon wanted to do something about it, immediately, and spent a while composing a text to his manager that began respectfully and deteriorated. Hunter watched him type and delete, type and delete. Part of him wanted to tell Dillon to send it, and part of him kept doing the math: twelve hours a week at seven twenty-five, and a manager who had other applicants. He understood both positions at once, which was uncomfortable, like standing in a doorway.

"You could ask about a raise after a couple months," Reda said. "That's what my dad did." Dillon said that was a beggar's strategy, and Reda said fine, beseech them then, if that was the word he preferred, and Dillon said it was not, and the argument collapsed into laughter somewhere around the word beseech, the tension draining out of the room.

What settled over the table after that was less a resolution than a detente. Dillon would finish out the summer at the sandwich shop and start looking elsewhere in the fall. Reda would keep her garden center hours and her father's commute. Hunter sat with his own check under the lamp and did not say what he was thinking, which was that he didn't know yet whether he would stay at Rinaldi's and ask, or leave and cross the line, or whether either choice added up to anything he could defend out loud.

His mother came in with a bowl she was drying and glanced at the three stubs still laid out on the wood. "You split a check three ways?" she asked.

"We were comparing," Hunter said, and swept them into his hand before she could read the numbers. He slid Reda hers back into its bag and Dillon his back into quarters, and put his own in the drawer where his passport was, flat under the county map he'd kept from a school project, the state line running through it thin and blue.

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera; they remarried the following year.
story:
Jessica had spread the print of The Two Fridas across the picnic table and weighted its corners with stones from her mother's garden bed, because the afternoon wind kept trying to take it. The assignment from Ms. Hoffmann was due Monday: a formal critique of colour, composition and symbolism, no biography, no gossip about the artist's life, just what the painting itself could be seen to do. Jessica had written half a page. Then she had crossed out the half page.

Tavin came through the gap in the fence the way he always did, without knocking, holding two popsicles he'd taken from his own freezer. "You're doing homework in the yard," he said. "In August."

"I'm doing it everywhere. It's following me." She took the popsicle anyway. Tavin's own want arrived with him, as usual, inside the first minute of conversation: there was a show on Saturday, three bands, one of them good, and he needed a yes or a no because his cousin was driving and the car had five seats and no patience for late decisions. Jessica said maybe, which she knew was not an answer, and turned back to the painting.

"Okay, so tell me what you see," she said, because Ms. Hoffmann had told them that articulating to another person was a way of testing whether you were actually looking. "Two women sitting on a bench. Same face. The one on the left is in a white European dress, the one on the right in a Tehuana dress, that's traditional Mexican. The European one has had her heart cut out, you can see the anatomy, and she's holding a little pair of scissors that just did it. Blood drips down the white dress onto the ground. The other Frida holds a small portrait in her hand, and there's a vein running between them, joining their hearts."

"That's grim," Tavin said, sucking his popsicle.

"That's not analysis, that's plot. I need to say what the colour does. The ground is this barren tan, the sky is churning grey and white, and then the red of the blood and the red of the exposed heart are the only saturated colour in the whole picture. That's the thing. The composition is symmetrical, almost flat, like an icon, and the one point of asymmetry is that the left Frida is bleeding out and the right one isn't. The symbolism has to be about a self split in two, one side emptied, one side still holding the beloved's picture. But I can't say which side Kahlo is asking us to trust, or whether she's asking at all." Jessica pressed the stone down harder on the corner of the print. "Or whether the painting is just solipsism. Two versions of the same person talking to each other with nobody else in the room. Is that a weakness or the whole point?"

Tavin said, "Is Saturday a yes?"

"Did you hear anything I just said?"

"You said a lot of words at my face and one of them was about needing a decision, so I'm choosing to believe it was about Saturday."

She laughed despite herself and looked back at the print, and at her laptop lying open on the table, and it was the laptop that changed everything, because she had scrolled to the museum page to check the dimensions for her formal notes and there, under the image, in small grey type, was the date. 1939. She typed 1939 into the search bar, half knowing what she would find, and found it: Kahlo painted The Two Fridas in 1939, the year she divorced the muralist Diego Rivera. They remarried the following year.

She sat back on the bench so fast that a stone slipped and the wind lifted the corner of the print, and she had to interpose her hand flat against the paper to hold it down. "Tavin. The little portrait in the right Frida's hand. That's him. That's Rivera. She painted this the year they divorced."

"Okay," Tavin said carefully, in the voice of someone watching a stick of dynamite decide whether to go off.

"No, it matters. I had this whole reading where the painting was about the self divided, European versus Mexican, alone versus accompanied, and it is, but the date turns it. The bleeding Frida is the one whose vein has been severed, the artery that used to run to the portrait has been cut by her own scissors. She's not just split. She's newly split. This is a divorce painting. And then they got remarried the following year, so whatever certainty the painting has, she undid it, or complicated it, or survived past it, and I don't know which verb to use." Jessica pulled the laptop closer and began typing, fast, the way she did when a sentence arrived before she was ready for it. "My critique was going to say the symmetry creates stability and the blood undermines it. Now I think the undermining is the subject. The painting knows less than it pretends to. The composition is confident and the content is not."

From the kitchen window, her mother's voice came out querulous across the grass, asking whether anyone had seen her reading glasses, and Jessica called back that they were on the picnic table, which they were not, and by the time she had thought to check, Tavin had picked them up off the grill cover and was waving them like a small trophy.

"Saturday," he said, holding the glasses just out of reach, a negotiation in progress. "You get an answer out of me about your painting lady, I get one out of you."

"That's not a fair trade."

"It's the only trade on the table."

Jessica looked at the print, at the two women holding hands on the bench while one of them bled, at the date still glowing on the screen. The painting said 1939 and said it plainly, and everything after that she would have to argue for. "Fine," she said. "Saturday's a yes. Now give me my mom's glasses before she comes out here."

Tavin set the glasses down beside the stones, then leaned over the print, studying it properly for the first time. "The one on the left," he said, pointing. "She looks like she's the strong one, holding the scissors. Like it was her choice."

Jessica stopped typing. She looked at the left Frida, at the small deliberate hand and the thin line of red. "I have to rewrite my second paragraph," she said, and reached for the stone.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Spike tape is coloured tape used to mark where furniture and actors should be placed on the stage floor.
story:
The black box theatre smelled of dust and cold coffee, and Alexandra stood at the edge of it holding a binder she had annotated until the margins gave out. Mr. Asante had given her the one-act in September with only two instructions: the actors must be off book by the second week of November, and the sofa must stop wandering. The second instruction had seemed like a joke. It was not.

The sofa was the problem she could see. Every rehearsal, Esme and Alannah dragged it to a new spot, three feet stage left, then two feet back, then diagonally toward the wings as though the furniture itself were undecided about the scene. What Alexandra could not see was the other problem, the one underneath, which was that Alannah had stopped speaking to her outside of rehearsal entirely, and spoke to her inside rehearsal only in the flat voice of someone fulfilling an obligation.

"From the top of page nine," Alexandra called. "Alannah, you cross to the window after he says the line about the river."

"I know where I cross," Alannah said.

The play was about two sisters arguing over who would keep the family's house on the water, and the whole set was meant to feel riparian, the director's note in the script said, wet and green and bordered, which was why Mr. Asante had hung grey-blue fabric along the back wall and set a low bench by the window to suggest a dock. Alexandra had chosen it partly for that, the way the setting would do half her work for her, and partly because she had believed, in September, that directing a play with Alannah would repair whatever September had broken. That belief had not survived contact with October.

They ran page nine. Esme delivered the line about the river with real feeling, because Esme delivered everything with real feeling, and Alannah crossed to the window four beats early, so that the moment Esme turned to find her sister gone, her sister was already there, and the beat collapsed like a tent with one pole missing.

"Stop," Alexandra said, then, quieter, "sorry. Hold. Alannah, you're leaving before the line lands. The whole point is that he says it to your back."

"You told me to cross after the line. I crossed after the line."

"You crossed after the first word of the line."

Alannah set her jaw and looked at the floor, and Alexandra felt the old reflex, the one from before the rift, which was to soften the note into a compliment and let the timing slide. She had spent three years metabolizing every disagreement that way, swallowing the correction so nothing ever surfaced. She did not want to direct like that. She also did not want to lose Alannah entirely, and those two wants sat in her like two people sharing a too-small sofa.

"Let's mark it," she said, and knelt beside the window bench with a roll of coloured tape she had found in the props cabinet, fluorescent pink, half-used, wound around a pencil. She tore a short strip and pressed it to the floor at the spot where Alannah's cross should begin, and another where it should end, near the grey-blue fabric. "Start on the pink."

"What is that, even?" Esme asked, crouching to look at it.

"Spike tape," Alexandra said. "It marks where stuff goes. Actors, furniture, all of it."

"You're spiking me to the floor," Alannah said. It was the closest thing to a joke she had offered in two weeks.

"You're spiking yourself," Alexandra said. "I'm just agreeing on where."

They ran it again, and this time Alannah waited, all four beats, her stillness doing the work the early crossing had buried, and when she finally moved, sharp and hurt, onto the pink X, Esme's turn caught her mid-cross and the moment landed so cleanly that Alexandra heard herself exhale. She spiked the sofa next, two strips at its casters, and the bench, and the door frame where the absent brother was forever almost entering.

Afterward, while Esme gathered her bag and pretended not to listen, Alexandra said, "I know you're angry at me. I've been directing around it for three weeks and it's making the play worse, and I think it's making us worse, and I don't actually know how to fix either thing." It was the least softened sentence she had ever spoken to Alannah, and it hung in the empty theatre with the lights still up.

Alannah peeled the pink strip off the floor at the window, carefully, and held it between two fingers as though it were evidence. "You could have just said something in October," she said. "Instead of arranging my blocking so I'd have to stand near you."

"I didn't do that."

"You did it twice."

Alexandra went back through the blocking in her head, page four, page eleven, and found that it was true, or true enough, some instinct in her had placed the sisters side by side at the table, side by side at the window, over and over, without her ever admitting it was a message. She considered denying it. She considered apologizing for the wrong thing. What she said was, "Then take the cross you want on page nine and I'll spike it wherever you choose."

Alannah looked at her for a long moment, then crossed to the window and stood where the pink X had been, on the exact spot, but this time by her own decision. She pointed at the floor. "Here," she said, and held out her hand for the tape.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
The registration page asked for her date of birth three times, and Kaylee typed it three times as though the website might change its mind about her. Her eighteenth birthday had arrived in March like a package she had tracked for years, and now, in the kitchen light of a Tuesday evening, she was finally eligible to vote in her first federal election. Her laptop fan hummed. Her mother was in the other room arguing with the dishwasher.

She texted Eve first, because Eve had already registered and considered herself, at eighteen and two months, a veteran of democracy. "Did you know we've only been allowed to do this since 1970?" Eve wrote back, almost instantly, the way she answered everything, as though the phone were an extension of her hand. "Before that you had to be 21. My gran voted in that election. She says the young people ruined everything." Kaylee laughed, then reread the message. Nineteen seventy. It sounded recent and ancient at once, like the year her parents were born, which it nearly was. People her age had been turned away from polling stations within her own mother's lifetime, and her mother was not, whatever she claimed, remotely old.

The thought was tangential, she knew, to the actual decision in front of her, which was which candidate to support, and yet she could not stop turning it over. She opened a second tab and verified it on a government archive, because Eve, though confident, was not a source. Lowered from twenty-one to eighteen, in 1970. She sat with that for a moment. Someone had fought for it, presumably; someone had stood in a room and argued that eighteen-year-olds, who could sign contracts and be drafted and be tried as adults, deserved a ballot. That part the archive did not dwell on, and she did not chase it.

Ishaan called while she was on the candidates' pages. He wanted to talk about the debate, or what he called the debate, which was mostly him performing the parts he had found ridiculous. "That man blamed the housing crisis on immigrants," he said. "With his whole chest." Kaylee propped the phone against the salt shaker and let him go. He was funny, and she needed the funny, because the policy documents were dense enough to resuscitate her insomnia. She had promised herself she would read them all, every plank, and she had made this promise the way she made all promises to herself at midnight, with total conviction and no follow-through strategy.

"You're overthinking it," Ishaan said when she admitted she had four tabs open and no decision. "Just vote for whoever your parents vote for, that's what everyone does." "That is not what everyone does." "Fine, it's what I did." She could hear him grinning. But his flippancy sat oddly beside what she had learned an hour earlier, that the right she was exercising was younger than her gran's opinions, that it had not always existed and therefore, she supposed, could be treated as though it had never been earned. She did not say any of this. She said, "Your parents vote for the guy who blamed housing on immigrants?" A pause. "We're having a complicated evening," Ishaan said.

The complication, when she finally named it to herself, was that two instincts in her were pulling in opposite directions. One was Mr. Hughes's, from Grade Ten civics, though he had never lectured; he had only put a quotation on the board and let it sit there, something about how an uninformed vote was not a virtue. The other instinct was newer and hotter, something Eve had said at lunch, that treating politics like homework was how people talked themselves out of participating at all. Both felt true. She could not make them agree, and she was beginning to suspect they never would, that voting might be exactly the place where an honest person did the math and still had to round.

She read the housing plans side by side. She read the climate commitments, which one candidate stated in numbers and the other stated in adjectives, and the adjectives, she noticed, could be rearranged to mean anything, a kind of chicanery she was starting to spot the way one spots a mislabeled price tag. Outside, a neighbor's dog announced itself to the whole street. Her mother appeared in the doorway, dish towel over one shoulder, and asked what she was doing. "Voting," Kaylee said. "It's a whole thing." Her mother looked at the four open tabs, the notes app glowing with bullet points, and said, "When I was your age, I couldn't have," and went back to the dishwasher before Kaylee could ask what she meant by the past tense, exactly.

In the end she filled out the registration and left the ballot decision for tomorrow, or for the walk to the polling station, or wherever it would finally decide to happen. Eve texted a photo of her own confirmation screen with the caption "civic icon." Kaylee sent back a thumbs up, then, after a minute, the link to the archive, the one with 1970 in it, and typed, "Read this before you brag." Then she closed the laptop, and the kitchen went quieter than it had been all evening, except for the dishwasher, which had apparently won its argument.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Aristotle named three means of persuasion: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, the logic of the argument.
story:
Grandmother's kitchen smelled of cardamom and old paper, and Annabelle spread her debate notes across the table where the placemats should have been. In nine days she would stand up in Mr. Sutherland's classroom and argue, for five minutes, entirely in French, whether cities should make public transit free. Nine days, one language she had studied for four years but never once used to fight.

She had worked all week at home, and the work had gone badly in a way she couldn't name. Her argument was solid. Free transit reduced congestion, saved money on fare collection, helped the poorest riders most. She had statistics, and French words for all of them, circled and recopied until her handwriting looked like someone else's. But when she read the draft aloud to her bedroom wall, something flattened out halfway through, and she kept talking anyway, the way you keep walking on a leg that has gone numb.

"You're at Grandmother's again," Alycia said on the phone that evening, meaning: with the good tea and no little brother. "Can I come Saturday? I'll time you. Jessie too."

"Bring the timer from the science lab," Annabelle said. "The one that doesn't tick."

Upstairs, in the study her grandfather had left more or less as he kept it, she was hunting for a French dictionary with a better verb section when she found the rhetoric book. It was small and green, its spine gone soft, and inside the cover he had written his name and a date from before she was born. She sat down on the floor with it, because the desk chair still held his sweater and moving it felt like a decision for somebody else to make.

The book was in English, which helped. On a page she opened to at random, under a heading about ancient Greece, she found a sentence she read three times: Aristotle named three means of persuasion. He called them ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, the logic of the argument.

Annabelle looked at her own notes, fanned out on the rug beside her. Congestion. Fare revenue. Ridership figures. Every point she had built was logic, and only logic. No wonder the draft went numb. She had written five minutes of proof for people who were not made of proof.

Saturday, Alycia and Jessie arrived with the lab timer and a lemon cake Grandmother cut into before anyone asked. Grandmother didn't speak French, but she understood the shape of the problem. "When I gave the eulogy for your grandfather," she said, setting down plates, "I did not use a single fact. I told them how he sang while he shelled peas." She went back to the kitchen, and Annabelle wrote sing while shelling peas in the margin of her notes and then, underneath, ethos. Who was she, that anyone should believe her? A sixteen-year-old who rode the bus every day, who had watched the number 14 skip her stop in the rain.

They dragged the kitchen chairs to the parlour, where the light was better, and Alycia held the timer like a starting gun. "Cinq minutes," Jessie said, because she took one semester of French and intended to use it.

Annabelle began in French, and this time she began differently, not with the fare revenue but with her own wet shoulders at the bus stop, the driver's face when she counted out coins. Her accent stumbled, and she let it. Jessie leaned forward. Halfway through, when she reached the statistics, Alycia stopped watching the timer and started watching her, and that was how Annabelle knew the argument had finally stood up.

"Vous êtes très bellicose," Jessie said afterward, pleased with herself.

"Is that good?" Annabelle asked, and Alycia laughed. "It means combative. Like you want to declare war on bus fares." Annabelle decided she would keep some of that ferocity but sand down the rest, because bellicose lost listeners, and pathos was not the same thing as volume.

"It's still all one side, though," Alycia said, honest the way she'd been honest since they were nine. "You say free transit helps poor riders. Someone will say the money has to come from somewhere, maybe from schools. Mr. Sutherland will poke at that."

Annabelle knew she was right, and knew something else too, which was that she hadn't decided yet where she truly stood. She believed in the free buses and she believed in the schools, and five minutes of French did not seem like enough room for both. Grandmother came in with more tea and heard the shape of it. "Your grandfather's first job, in the mill office, was basically a sinecure," she said. "They paid him to sit at a desk and look at a wall. He said real work makes you choose. He hated choosing." She refilled Jessie's cup without being asked, because Jessie always forgot to drink when she was excited.

They worked until the light went long and yellow. Alycia drafted a counterargument in English so Annabelle could knock it down in French; Jessie held the timer and mispronounced encouragement. When the girls finally packed up, Annabelle walked them to the gate, then went back inside and up to the study.

She sat cross-legged on the rug with the green book open on her knees and a fresh page in her lap, and at the top of the page she wrote, in careful French, the first line of the part she had not figured out yet.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995; its lead designer was James Gosling.
story:
The laptop battery died at four percent, so Anna commandeer the corner machine in the lab, the one with the wobbly spacebar, because her class file was due to Ms. Joseph by the end of the meeting and she was not going home without a green test bar. Coding club met Thursdays in the chemistry lab that smelled faintly of vinegar, nine students scattered among the sinks, and Anna had spent two of those Thursdays stuck on the same thing: a class in Java called Runner with private fields for name and pace, getter methods to read them, and a test that kept printing red.

She would tell anyone who asked that she understood the whole concept already, that it was only syntax tripping her up, and she told Alessio exactly that when he slid into the seat beside her. "The private fields are the easy part," she said. "It's the getters I keep fumbling."

"You said that last week," Alessio said, not unkindly, and pulled his own laptop toward him. "Last week you said the fields were the hard part."

She let that pass, because arguing with Alessio about what she had said last week was a losing sport. He remembered everything, including things she had only half said, and the half she had not said.

What she wanted, though she had not said this to anyone, was for Ms. Joseph to look at her test, nod once, and say something with perspicacity in it, something that showed she had looked at the code and seen the person who wrote it. Anna's older brother had gone through this club three years ago and Ms. Joseph had apparently told him he thought like an engineer. Anna wanted a sentence like that. She wanted it badly enough that she had, once, written a getter that returned the wrong field on purpose, so that when she fixed it, the fix would look like insight. That had been two weeks ago. It had not worked then either.

Quintin was across the table, on the robotics team laptop, arguing with nobody in particular about whether Java was too old to be teaching. "It feels antiquated," he said. "Like we're learning on something out of a museum."

"It's not that old," Alessio said.

"It's older than us," Quintin said. "Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995. It's literally older than every person in this room."

"Who even made it, though," Anna said, mostly to keep her hands from shaking over the keyboard while the file loaded.

"James Gosling was the lead designer," Alessio said, in the flat tone he used for facts, and went back to his screen. Anna looked at the date in the corner of Quintin's browser, at 1995 sitting there in the search result, and felt something small rearrange itself. Twenty-three years of people had written this language before she touched it. Somewhere it had been new, and someone had made it on purpose.

She typed the class again from a blank file, and this time, instead of copying the pattern from the board, she asked herself what the private keyword was protecting. Not hiding, exactly. Guarding, the way the supply closet was locked not because the beakers were secret but because unsupervised hands broke things. The getters were the supervised hands. She wrote getName and getPace, one line each, and for the first time the two ideas arrived together instead of fighting each other. Then she wrote the test, the part she had been treating as a formality, and actually read it: she had been calling getName and printing the result without ever checking it against anything, which meant the test had been passing vacuously all along. Red to green meant nothing if you never asked the question. She fixed the assertion, ran it, and the bar went green.

Ms. Joseph came around the tables with her clipboard, and when she reached Anna she leaned over the wobbly laptop and read for a long moment. "You test the getter against a literal," she said. "Most students your age just print and look."

"She wrote it herself," Alessio said. "From nothing, in like ten minutes."

Anna opened her mouth to say thank you, and then closed it, because she had not, not exactly. Two weeks ago she had committed a broken version to the shared folder, and last week Quintin had pushed a file over it, and she had just now rewritten the whole thing from blank. The green bar on the screen was hers, but the folder on the server held a version with someone else's fingerprint on it, and she had known that, and she had been letting herself not know it.

"Mostly myself," she said. "There's a version in the shared folder that isn't all mine. Quintin changed something in it last week and I never sorted out what."

Quintin looked up. "I fixed your constructor," he said. "It wasn't compiling. I left a note in the commit message."

"There's a commit message?"

"There's always a commit message," Quintin said, and turned his laptop so she could see it, a single line from Thursday of last week, sitting in the history like it had been waiting for her to look.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void.
story:
The porch light at Grandma's house came on before the sky had fully darkened, a small diurnal ritual Sienna had watched all her life, though tonight she barely noticed it because her laptop screen had just printed the word null for the third time in a row.

"Run it again," Amelia said from the kitchen doorway, a mug of Grandma's chamomile cooling in her hand.

"I ran it again. It's the same." Sienna turned the laptop so Amelia could see the test she had written, the one Mr. Morales had posted that morning and that was due by midnight. The assignment was to build a class called Song with private fields for title and artist, getter methods for each, and a small test class to prove the whole thing worked. Her test printed the title as null. The artist, too. Somewhere between her keyboard and the machine, the songs were empty.

Grandma shuffled past with her crossword and said, "When I was your age, a song was a record and it either played or it didn't."

"This one doesn't play," Sienna said. "That's the problem."

She scrolled up through her code. She had declared the fields private, exactly as instructed. She had written the getter methods, getTitle and getArtist, each returning its field. And she had written what she believed was a constructor, a block that took a title and an artist and set the fields equal to them. It looked right to her. It looked, if anything, tidier than Mr. Morales's example on the handout, because she had put void in front of it, the way she put void in front of every method that gave nothing back. She was proud of that consistency an hour ago. Now she stared at it and felt the pride curdle.

"Text Justice?" Amelia suggested. "He finished his already, I saw him flexing about it in the group chat."

"I don't want the answer." Sienna heard how stubborn it sounded even as she said it. She had spent the whole semester insisting she wanted to work things out alone, which had felt like integrity in September and felt more like stubbornness now, with the clock on her laptop reading 9:47. She pulled the handout toward her anyway, side by side with her own code, and made herself read the example line by line instead of skimming for the shape of it.

That was where she saw it. Mr. Morales's constructor had nothing in front of its name. No void, nothing. It was just the class name, twice: Song, then Song again with parentheses after it. She looked at her own version, at the void sitting there like a period at the end of the wrong sentence. A Java constructor has the same name as its class, she thought, and no return type, not even void. Not even void. The words rearranged something in her head. She had assumed the constructor was a method like any other, and methods announced what they returned. This was something else. This was a special thing with its own rule, and her tidy little void had made the machine treat it as just another method, one that happened to share the class's name, one that ran when called and was never called at all.

Her cursor hovered over the void. It occurred to her, strangely, that the mistake had been invisible to her precisely because it was so orderly. She had been so careful to make the code look uniform that she had never stopped to introspect, to turn around and ask what each piece was actually for.

She deleted the void and ran the test.

The screen printed a title. Then an artist. An actual song, whole, where an hour ago there had been nothing.

"Wait, that's it?" Amelia leaned over her shoulder. "You deleted one word?"

"One word." Sienna sat back. "It's kind of a travesty, honestly. I spent two hours on that."

"You spent two hours learning it, though." Amelia drained her mug. "Justice would've just sent you a screenshot and you'd have typed it in and learned nothing."

Sienna considered that. She had spent most of the semester believing that asking was cheaper than figuring, and that speed was the same thing as understanding, and both of those beliefs now seemed shakier than they had at dinner. Though she was honest enough to admit she didn't know where the line sat. If the deadline had been an hour earlier, she might have texted Justice and been glad of it. Maybe struggling was only virtuous when you had time for it. She filed the question away, unresolved, next to all the other things she was carrying to college in two years.

She added a second test, a third, checking that the getters returned what the constructor set. Grandma paused at the doorway on her way to bed and looked at the screen, at the rows of small words lit up in the dark room.

"Now it plays?" Grandma asked.

"Now it plays," Sienna said, and pressed Enter one more time to watch it happen.

fact: Artists commonly keep two versions of their statement: a short one of about 50 to 100 words and a longer one of about 500 to 1,000 words.
story:
The screen door of his grandfather's house still shrieked on its hinges, the way it had when Matthew was six, and he let it bang behind him as he carried his portfolio case into the kitchen. Ten drawings of hands were inside, all of hands: his grandfather's hands shelling peas, his own hands failing at a knot, a plaster hand he had photographed at the hospital when his grandmother went in for tests last spring. He had chosen hands because they were the one thing his grandfather, a taciturn man who answered questions in three words or fewer, actually talked about while working.

Ms. Sharma had given the class until Friday. Ten artworks, one theme, and an artist's statement to hold it together. Matthew spread the drawings across the kitchen table, weighting the corners with saucers from the drainboard, and tried to read them the way a stranger would. He had spent the whole drive out here ruminating on what the theme actually was, because "hands" was a subject, not a theme, and Ms. Sharma had underlined that distinction twice on the assignment sheet.

Casey arrived at noon, having biked eleven kilometres on the promise of lemonade and a look at the work. Casey was applying to the same summer program and had already finished a portfolio about urban wind, whatever that meant. They stood over the table, squinting. "These are good," Casey said, in the tone people used when they meant something more complicated than good. "But the program wants the statement in two places. Did you see?"

Matthew had not seen. Casey pulled up the application page on a cracked phone and handed it over. There was a box for a statement of about 50 to 100 words, for the wall card beside the exhibited work, and a separate upload demanding a longer one, 500 to 1,000 words, for the review committee. Matthew read it twice. He had written one statement, three hundred words, laboriously, and it fit neither box like a shoe fits neither foot.

"That's stupid," he said. "It's the same art."

"Artists do it all the time, apparently," Casey said, scrolling. "Short one for the wall, long one for the application."

His grandfather came in from the garden with mud on his cuffs and washed his hands at the sink without a word, which was his way of joining a conversation. Matthew watched the water run grey off the knuckles, the tendons shifting under the skin, and thought about the difference between what a person does and what a person says about what they do. The short statement, he realized, was like his grandfather: accurate, compressed, done. The long one had to be like the drawings themselves, which took time to look at.

He tried drafting the short version first, on a napkin because his notebook was in the car. Fifty words about hands, about gesture as a record of work. It came out flat. He tried again and got something almost honest: "I draw hands because they hold their history in the joints." Twenty-five words with room left, and he couldn't figure out what to do with the room. Casey suggested filling it with something about memory. Brianna, texted a photo of the napkin, wrote back a single line, "hedonism," which was a joke about an argument they had had in Ms. Sharma's class about whether art needed to be useful, and it didn't help at all, but it made him laugh, and laughing loosened something.

The long statement was worse, or better, depending on when he looked at it. He wrote four hundred words in the afternoon while Casey read a magazine on the porch and his grandfather moved through the rows of beans outside the window. In those four hundred words he found himself making claims he wasn't sure he believed, that the hand was a portrait of labour, that drawing was an act of respect. He deleted half of it. Then he wrote about the plaster cast, about not being able to tell whose hand it had been, and that part felt true, truer than any of the grand sentences, and he kept it.

By supper he had a short statement and a long one, and they disagreed with each other. The short one said the work was about gesture. The long one said it was about not knowing, about hands being anonymous records. He sat with the two of them side by side on the table and couldn't decide whether the disagreement was a failure or simply the truth, one thing you say quickly to a stranger passing a wall, another thing you say slowly to someone who will sit with it.

Casey leaned over his shoulder. "They contradict."

"I know."

"Is that allowed?"

Matthew looked out at his grandfather, who was washing his hands again at the outdoor tap, carefully, each finger. "I don't know," Matthew said. "I think maybe the short one is what I hoped the work was about, and the long one is what it's actually about."

He typed the shorter version into the application box first, watched the character count accept it, then attached the longer file without changing a word of either. His grandfather came in, looked at the ten drawings still spread across the table under their saucers, and picked up the one of his own hands shelling peas. He held it beside his hands, mud still dried in the creases. "You got the knuckles wrong," he said.
